newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Is the party over for booming Philippines?.
newsitem.headline: Is the party over for booming Philippines?.

text.p: The stock market is plunging, coorporate profits are at best dull, politics is looking murky again and people in the Philippines are asking if the party is over.
At the root of the unease is speculation over what lies ahead for the country as President Fidel Ramos begins the last year of his term and who will succeed him, analysts say.
Will he step down as the constitution demands or will he manoeuvre his way around it so he can continue to rule the rambunctious nation of 7,000 islands into the 21st century?

"Business is quite happy with the way Ramos has managed the economy. The main challenge now is for Ramos to show he is in command of the succession issue, that there will be no discontinuity or turbulence," University of the Philippines political science professor Alex Magno said on Sunday.
"Investor confidence could become shaky if major mistakes are made in politics or in the economy because...of capital flight (from the stock market). There's that worry."

From flat growth when Ramos took over in 1992, the country has bounced to become Asia's newest tiger economy, posting an unprecedented five straight years of growth. Economists project growth this year will be just above last year's 6.8 percent.

Clouds gathered last month after the stock market, touted in 1993 as one of Asia's star performers, registered its biggest drop in over two years as investors fled on fears of a property bust as in Thailand.
The bleeding at the bourse unnerved the peso, forcing the Central Bank to sell dollars and raise interest rates.
Disappointing first-quarter results by some leading companies also dimmed the landscape.
"Confidence has faltered as underlying economic problems endemic to a growing economy have become manifest," analyst Jerry Barican wrote in the Manila Standard newspaper.
"But this is for the best if our investors and managers learn from their mistakes and position themselves more competitively for the future. The party couldn't last forever."
Is the party over?
Not quite, Ramos insists. "Stick with us," he said in a recent speech. "The best is yet come."
Many analysts agree with Ramos that the economy is not in any major trouble and that comparisons with Thailand are far-fetched.

"We've been through worse things and always bounced back towards the centre," analyst Nelson Navarro said. "I think not even the worst scenario indicates the growth rate would be badly hit. The fundamentals are still on the side of stability."
Much of the concern centres on the toll politics could take on Ramos's reform programme as Filipinos prepare for presidential elections in May 1998.

Despite Ramos's public pledges that he will step down when his term ends in June next year, a vociferous opposition and a combative media have accused him of instigating a campaign to change the constitution so he can run for re-election.
A hangover of Ferdinand Marcos's harsh 20-year rule, which came to an abrupt end in 1986, the constitution now limits a president to only one six-year term.
"What worries people is the big picture. Is Ramos staying on? If not, can he manage the transition?" Navarro said. "You keep running into question marks. Businessmen don't like question marks."
Guillermo Luz, executive director of the prestigious Makati Business Club, says he worries that excessive politicking in the run-up to the 1998 elections may derail economic momentum.
"The basic weakness I see is that we end up 80 percent of our time on politics and forget about the economy for the next 12 months. That's a real danger," Luz told Reuters.
"We've worked this hard we can't fall back again... We have a success to protect."
Analyst Magno sees Ramos treading a political tightrope as he seeks to calm business.

"On the one hand, he has to parry fears of a new dictatorship or strongman rule which is being exploited by the opposition, but on the other hand, he has to convince business that he has his firm hand in the succession problem."
